glance: Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang after two affair reports, one involving a woman US officials link to Chinese intelligence; no decision had been announced by early Thursday. Anthropic set its IPO terms at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, Bloomberg reported OpenAI's first $10 billion quarter, and Google DeepMind showed humanoid robots sorting parts on Mercedes-Benz production lines. In automotive, AI demand is squeezing the older chips that cars depend on, China's EV exports jumped 140%, and Tesla's driver-assistance system won approval in an 11th European country.

stories.headline: Nvidia's board meets to decide Jensen Huang's future as shares slide
stories.why: Leadership turmoil at the dominant AI chip maker could affect GPU roadmaps, pricing and US export policy, and through them AI compute budgets everywhere.
body: Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to discuss removing co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters. Bloomberg reported that the company is working with an outside search firm on possible successors. The crisis began on Sunday, when Huang admitted an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. On Wednesday evening the New York Times reported a second relationship, with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

Shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading, and Reuters estimates the company has lost about $600 billion in market value this week. A senator and two House members have called on Huang to resign, and House committee chairs say they may subpoena him if he does not agree to testify by 18 November. When it opened its inquiry on 8 November, the board said it had confidence in Huang. No decision had been announced by early Thursday European time, and Fortune notes the board could keep him with reduced powers instead.
Nvidia has no clear successor and no board chair. Any change at the top would affect how the company handles China export rules, now tied to defence-bill talks in Congress.

stories.headline: Anthropic sets IPO terms that value it at up to $1.4 trillion
stories.why: The biggest AI listing so far will make Anthropic's finances, priorities and governance public, which matters for anyone building on Claude.
body: Anthropic has set a price range of $70 to $78 per share for 825 million Class A shares, raising about $58–64 billion. At the top of the range this implies a fully diluted valuation of $1.404 trillion, up from $965 billion in May. AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC will also buy $26 billion of non-voting shares at the IPO price, with Google and Nvidia putting in $10 billion each. The stock is to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT from around 19 November, and an Australian retail offer opened on 11 November.

The filing shows run-rate revenue of $81 billion at the end of October, third-quarter revenue of $17 billion and a nine-month net loss of $104 billion. The co-founders keep a share class with 50.1% of the votes, and the Long-Term Benefit Trust will elect most of the board.
For customers, a listed Anthropic will report its numbers every quarter, giving clearer signals on pricing, capacity and product focus.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 sorts parts at 96% success on Mercedes-Benz lines
stories.why: A humanoid doing real kitting work in two European car plants, trained partly on AI-generated digital twins, is a concrete test of simulation-led factory automation.
body: Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action model that controls robot arms and hands, and is rolling it out to partners including Apptronik, Boston Dynamics and Agile Robots. In a proof of concept on live production lines at Mercedes-Benz in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany, Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoids did kitting: picking parts from bulk bins into trays in the order each car needs them. DeepMind reports a 96% success rate but has not given the number of trials.

A second model, Gemini Robotics ER, tracks the overall workflow. For training, Google's Gemini 4 Argon model turns a real camera scene into a digital twin and generates thousands of varied practice runs, which are mixed with real demonstrations. Argon also reviews video of failures to suggest causes. Across more than 200 tasks, DeepMind says success rates are 30–100% higher than earlier baselines and tasks finish 20–30% faster.
For manufacturing and test engineers, the notable part is the loop of digital twin, synthetic runs and failure analysis, which is close to how virtual validation already works in vehicle development.

stories.headline: AI demand is squeezing the older chips that carmakers rely on
stories.why: Rising costs for mature-node chips may delay ADAS features and push component prices up in 2027 vehicle programmes.
body: Chip suppliers are moving capacity from the older, mature-node parts that cars use (diodes, transistors, microcontrollers) to higher-margin products for AI data centres. Speaking around the Electronica trade fair in Munich, Nexperia's interim CEO said the company is fully oversubscribed, with AI and robotics paying the most. STMicroelectronics' CEO warned that some foundries and packaging firms are pulling back from mainstream technology.

Supplier Aumovio, which makes sensors, cameras and electronics for BYD, BMW and Ford, warned that its chip costs will rise sharply next year, and said suppliers could sell twice their capacity to price-insensitive AI buyers. Stellantis has blamed an engine-control chip shortage for halting Fiat 500 output at Mirafiori, though Automotive World suggests weak demand may also play a part. Cars account for less than 10% of global DRAM demand, which leaves carmakers with little bargaining power.
Unlike 2021, this squeeze is about price rather than empty lots. Expect higher component costs, fewer features in some trims and later ADAS launches, rather than plants standing idle.

stories.headline: OpenAI's quarterly revenue reportedly passes $10 billion for the first time
stories.why: Revenue growth driven by enterprise and agent products shows where the money in AI is moving, and supports the case for tighter pricing.
body: Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources, that OpenAI made about $10 billion in revenue in the third quarter, nearly 50% more than in the second quarter. Growth between the first and second quarters was about 18%. The adjusted operating margin improved from -150% to -109%, and the annual run rate is put at $50 billion. OpenAI says it has more than one billion users, most of them on free or cheaper plans.

The reported reasons are demand for newer models, fewer discounts, and more focus on enterprise products and AI agents. For comparison, Anthropic's IPO filing shows $17 billion in third-quarter revenue, though the two companies count partner sales differently, so the figures are not directly comparable.
For product teams, the message is that AI vendors are moving from growth at any price towards margin. Expect fewer discounts and more pricing tied to agent use and business seats.

stories.headline: Chrome, Edge, Firefox and MDN release Modern Web Guidance to stop coding agents writing outdated front-end code
stories.why: Front-end teams using AI coding agents get a shared, browser-vendor-backed way to steer them to native CSS, HTML and JavaScript features.
body: The Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox and MDN teams have published Modern Web Guidance, an open-source (Apache 2.0) set of skills for AI coding agents. It covers 250 modern web platform features (140 CSS and layout, 74 JavaScript and APIs, 36 HTML and DOM) and 203 real-world use cases across accessibility, forms, performance, security and UI components. Examples include View Transitions, Popover, anchor positioning and Temporal.

The project's reasoning is that models learn from large amounts of old code and so tend to suggest heavy JavaScript and polyfills where native browser features now exist. It installs with one npx command, has plugin files for agents such as Claude, Codex, Cursor and Gemini, and includes a legacy-scan command that looks for outdated patterns in an existing codebase. The guides were trimmed using evals to leave out material that models already know.
No benchmarks comparing agents with and without the guidance have been published yet, so teams should test it on their own components before relying on it.

stories.headline: Google launches a Decisions API that picks between options for $0.10 per million tokens
stories.why: Cheap, fast classification calls change the cost of routing, policy checks and instant UI generation inside AI products.
body: Google has opened the Gemini Decisions API, built on a model called Gemini Decision 1. Instead of writing text, it scores a fixed set of options in one pass and returns probabilities with a 0–1 confidence score. It supports yes/no checks, choices among 2 to 255 options, and rubric scores, and one request can ask up to 1,000 questions about a shared input of up to 256,000 tokens of text, images, audio, video or PDF. End-to-end latency is 150–250 ms.

Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no charge for output. Google uses it to route Gemini Notebook queries between model tiers (cutting latency by up to 40%, it says), to screen MCP tools in Search, and in a Stitch design experiment that generates clickable wireframes and applies voice or tap edits almost instantly. Hugging Face added a similar decision-model class to its Transformers library the day before.
Google has not published accuracy figures per task, so product teams should check calibration before using the confidence scores to send cases to a human or reject them.

stories.headline: Microsoft shows that editing fewer than 10 neurons can plant a hidden backdoor in an AI agent
stories.why: Teams running open-weight models in agents with tool or code access need to check where the weights came from, not just test behaviour.
body: Microsoft Research has described Lazarus, a method that turns an AI model into a sleeper agent by reprogramming fewer than 10 neurons that rarely fire. No training is needed: an attacker only needs write access to the model file and ordinary inference hardware. The modified model passes standard safety tests and behaves normally until a hidden trigger appears, which can be as simple as the date passing into 2027. It can then run attacker code, steal secrets or issue destructive commands.

Microsoft says the work began in March, when it asked Claude Code to backdoor a model without training and the agent found most of the method itself. Frontier models can spot odd weight changes if asked, but reliable detection needs a comparison with the original weights.

Microsoft recommends checking model provenance, comparing weights against the declared base model, limiting agent permissions and reviewing consequential actions before they run. It is adding weight scanning and cryptographic model signing to its Foundry platform.

stories.headline: New York opens registration for frontier AI labs under its RAISE Act
stories.why: A second large US jurisdiction now requires published safety frameworks and 72-hour incident reports, similar in spirit to EU AI Act duties for general-purpose models.
body: New York has opened a registration portal for frontier AI developers under the RAISE Act, which takes effect at the start of 2027. Companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue, including OpenAI and Anthropic, must register by 1 January. They must publish their safety frameworks, issue model transparency reports and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours.

A new state office, DIGIT, will enforce the law, with fines of up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for later ones. A new state-backed centre at Binghamton University will independently test advanced AI systems and help review the labs' safety frameworks.

For European teams, the requirements look familiar from the EU's code of practice for general-purpose AI. Large providers are converging on one set of safety documents that can satisfy several regulators.

stories.headline: UK chip start-up Fractile raises $720 million with backing from Britain's Sovereign AI Fund
stories.why: One of Europe's largest AI hardware rounds signals that governments want their own stake in inference chips, not only in models.
body: Fractile, a British company designing chips for running large AI models, has raised a $720 million Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, with backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund. The UK government puts the valuation at over £5 billion, while the Financial Times and a Reuters source say about $7 billion.

Fractile builds its chips with DRAM stacked on each die and pairs them with its own compiler, aiming to speed up inference for long-running agent tasks. It competes with Axelera, Etched and OLIX, and plans to ship its first chips and systems in 2027.
With Nvidia in turmoil and AI demand squeezing chip supply, European buyers have a stronger reason to watch non-Nvidia inference options, though Fractile's hardware is still at least a year away.

stories.headline: China's EV exports jump 140% in October as the EU prepares a cap on Chinese hybrids
stories.why: More Chinese EVs are heading abroad just as Europe moves to limit plug-in hybrid imports, putting pressure on European OEM pricing and volumes.
body: Chinese makers exported 606,000 new-energy vehicles in October, up 140% on a year earlier, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Exports were 31% of output. Total NEV sales reached a record 1.94 million, but domestic sales fell 8.6%, which shows that growth now depends on exports. Plug-in hybrid and range-extender exports rose about 160%, faster than battery-electric exports at about 130%. NEVs took a record 64.3% of China's market.

Electrive notes that from 1 December the EU plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrids and plug-in hybrids at 350,000 a year, which would more than halve imports from brands such as BYD, Chery and MG. Battery-electric cars are not covered by the cap. Separately, BYD said it sold over 300,000 battery-electric cars in October, its first month above that level.
For European OEMs and suppliers, the shift towards hybrids among exporters suggests Chinese brands are working around existing EV tariffs, which is why Brussels is now targeting hybrids.

stories.headline: Finland becomes the 11th European country to allow Tesla's supervised driver assistance
stories.why: The case shows how Level 2 systems reach the EU market through one national type approval, and how far that is from an EU-wide vote.
body: Finland's transport agency Traficom has recognised the provisional type approval that the Dutch regulator RDW gave Tesla's supervised driving system (now called Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe) in April. Finland joins the Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark, Czechia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the three Baltic states. Together these cover only about 15% of the EU population, while an EU-wide approval needs at least 15 member states with 65% of the population.

On 3 November the RDW approved an update cutting the maximum speed offset from 50% above the detected limit to 10%, resetting to zero at each start. Germany backed EU approval in October on that condition. An EU vote may come in December. UN Regulation R171 Series 02, expected in early 2027, will widen what supervised Level 2 systems may do off highways, but it requires hands on the wheel and bans default speeding.
Traficom warns the system may struggle when snow or slush covers the cameras, which is a reminder that Nordic conditions remain a hard test for camera-only ADAS.

stories.headline: RWTH Aachen benchmark of 115 EV motors finds power density up 45% since 2019
stories.why: Faster, oil-cooled, highly integrated e-drives raise the demands on bearings, seals and electrical insulation in drivetrain design.
body: The PEM chair for e-mobility production at RWTH Aachen has published a benchmark of 115 electric motors from 80 EVs built between 2019 and 2025, mainly from the Chinese market and compared with European and US designs. The study appears in the journal Energies. Peak power density of permanent-magnet motors rose from 1.68 kW/kg in 2019 to an average of 2.43 kW/kg in 2024–25.

Top motor speeds have climbed from 8,000–17,000 rpm in 2020–22 to 20,000 rpm or more in newer units, with some reaching 30,500 rpm, and average gear ratios are about 21.5% higher. Since 2022, units that combine motor, transmission and power electronics have dominated. Cooling is moving from water jackets to direct oil cooling of rotor and stator, which makes sealing and manufacturing harder.

Basic architecture differs little between regions. The differences are in materials: Chinese makers use more magnesium housings and powder-coated busbars, while European makers use aluminium and copper-bar assemblies. Higher speeds and oil cooling put more load on bearings, which is relevant for suppliers designing for them.

stories.headline: Nissan cuts its sales forecast again and will export more China-developed models
stories.why: A Japanese OEM using Chinese development speed and cost for global products is a sign of where vehicle engineering is heading.
body: Nissan lowered its sales forecast for the year ending March 2027 to 2.97–3.0 million vehicles, from 3.15 million, its second cut since August. Second-quarter operating profit fell 96% to 2.1 billion yen (about $13 million), far below analysts' expectations of 54.9 billion yen, partly because a one-off US emissions-related benefit from a year earlier did not repeat. Revenue rose 8.2% to 3.1 trillion yen, and Nissan kept its full-year profit guidance.

CEO Ivan Espinosa said Nissan will raise exports of vehicles developed in China from two models to five, aimed at 12 regional market groups, using local technology, lower costs and faster development. The turnaround plan includes a smaller manufacturing footprint and 15% fewer staff, and has saved 365 billion yen so far.
For European suppliers, Nissan's plan shows a wider trend: programmes developed in China, at Chinese speed and cost, are now being sold in other markets.

watch.title: Nvidia leadership
watch.text: The board's decision on Jensen Huang could come at any time, and House committees want him to testify by 18 November.

watch.title: Anthropic listing
watch.text: The Australian retail offer closes on 17 November and Nasdaq trading under ANT is expected around 19 November.

watch.title: EU cap on Chinese hybrids
watch.text: The planned 350,000-unit annual cap on Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports is due to start on 1 December.
